query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy‐alloy multilayer protective coatings, the engineered chemical and crystallographic interfaces act as effective barriers to dislocation climb and grain‐boundary sliding, thereby slowing diffusion‐mediated plastic deformation (creep) compared to a homogeneous single‐layer HEA coating.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanocrystalline multilayer coating composed of alternating HEA layers (with subtly different compositions or phase structures, for example, alternating BCC/HCP or BCC/FCC layers) having as-deposited uniform microstructure and well-defined interfaces.
generation.intervention: Fabricate two sets of coatings: one multilayer architecture with controlled alternating layers and one monolithic (single-layer) HEA coating with the same overall chemistry and thickness.
generation.conditions: Subject both sets to high-temperature, sustained load conditions (e.g., 750–850 °C under constant stress) where diffusion and dislocation climb control creep kinetics.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer interfaces—regions with chemical and crystallographic discontinuities—that pin dislocations, impede their climb, and disrupt continuous diffusion pathways necessary for time-dependent deformation.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained load at high temperature, dislocation motion responsible for creep is slowed because dislocations are stopped or deflected at the interfaces; these barriers raise the activation energy for dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding, thus reducing the overall creep rate compared to a homogeneous structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayer coatings will show a delayed onset of accelerated creep, lower steady-state creep rates, and reduced total strain accumulation over time relative to monolithic coatings of the same overall composition and thickness.
generation.baseline: A monolithic HEA coating with the same overall chemistry and thickness, but without engineered alternating interfaces.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be most pronounced under conditions where diffusion-controlled creep is dominant (elevated temperatures, typically when grain-boundary and dislocation climb processes prevail) and when the individual layer thicknesses are on the order of tens of nanometers; at lower temperatures or for thicker layers (reducing the interface density), the benefit may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The extent to which residual stresses at interfaces, potential phase transformations, or interdiffusion during service might modify the barrier effect of the interfaces is not fully established. Moreover, the quantitative magnitude of the creep reductions may vary with the specific HEA system and multilayer design.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical sets of coatings on substrates: one group with a multilayer HEA architecture (with alternating nanocrystalline layers of ~20–50 nm thickness) and another group with a monolithic HEA layer (same overall thickness and chemistry). Subject both groups to constant-load (creep) tests at 750–850 °C for an extended period (e.g., several tens of hours). Periodically measure the accumulated strain and evaluate the microstructural evolution (using TEM and XRD) to assess dislocation activity and interface integrity.
measurements: Time-dependent strain (creep curves) using high-temperature dilatometry or in situ indentation
Dislocation density and distribution via TEM
Interface quality and layer integrity via cross-sectional SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in steady-state creep rates and cumulative strain (or if the dislocation architectures are similar to those in the monolithic coatings) under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that the multilayer interfaces improve resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation would be falsified.

System: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 (equiatomic atomic percentages). Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests at room temperature, and creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa loads. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs.
